segments.text: Since studying an entire population is usually impractical, statistics relies on drawing conclusions from a representative sample — this chapter covers how samples should be drawn and how sample-based statistics behave, providing the theoretical bridge to formal inference in Chapter 7.
is the complete set of individuals or items of interest; a
is a subset of the population actually observed. A
is a numerical characteristic of the population (usually unknown, and the actual target of investigation, e.g., the true population mean, μ); a
is the corresponding numerical characteristic calculated from the sample (e.g., the sample mean, x̄), used to estimate the unknown parameter.
gives every possible sample of a given size an equal chance of selection.

divides the population into relevant subgroups (strata) and samples separately (often proportionally) from each, ensuring representation of every important subgroup and typically improving precision when the strata differ meaningfully from each other.
selects every kth individual from an ordered list after a random starting point.

divides the population into naturally occurring groups (clusters), randomly selects entire clusters, and samples all (or a further sample of) individuals within the chosen clusters — often more practical and cost-effective for geographically dispersed populations, though generally less statistically efficient than stratified sampling for a given sample size.

is the unavoidable difference between a sample statistic and the true population parameter, arising simply because a sample is not the entire population — it can be reduced (though never eliminated) by increasing sample size.

arises from flaws in the data collection process itself — such as measurement error, non-response bias (certain types of people systematically failing to respond), or undercoverage (some part of the population having no chance of being selected at all) — and, critically, is not reduced by simply increasing sample size, since a larger flawed sample simply repeats the same flaw more often.

is the probability distribution of a statistic (such as the sample mean) computed over all possible samples of a given size drawn from the population — a theoretical construct essential for inference, since it describes how much a sample statistic would be expected to vary from sample to sample purely by chance, providing the basis for assessing how reliable any single observed sample statistic actually is.

states that, for a sufficiently large sample size, the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the shape of the original population’s distribution — a remarkably powerful result that justifies using normal-distribution-based methods (confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, Chapter 7) even when the underlying population itself is not normally distributed.

balances the desired precision (a smaller standard error, achieved with a larger sample) against practical constraints of cost, time, and feasibility — formal sample-size calculations typically specify a desired margin of error and confidence level in advance and solve for the required n. Good

requires deliberately anticipating and minimising non-sampling error sources (careful, unambiguous question wording, appropriate sampling frame, and strategies to maximise response rate) since, as established in point 3, these errors cannot be corrected after the fact simply by collecting more data.

items.text: A statistic (from a sample) estimates a parameter (of the population); the four common probability sampling methods (simple random, stratified, systematic, cluster) differ in structure and typical efficiency.
Sampling error is unavoidable but shrinks with larger samples; non-sampling error stems from flawed data collection and is not fixed by increasing sample size.
A sampling distribution describes how a statistic varies across all possible samples, underlying the standard error and all of formal statistical inference.
The Central Limit Theorem’s power lies in guaranteeing approximate normality of the sample mean’s distribution for large samples, regardless of the original population’s shape.
Sample-size determination and careful survey design both aim to control precision and error, but only sample size addresses sampling error — survey design must separately address non-sampling error.
